items.followUp: Derive the second equation of motion using a velocity-time graph.

rubric.why: Displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium.
rubric.description: Writes the displacement as the area of the trapezium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct area relation.

rubric.why: This uses the definition of acceleration to express time in terms of the velocities and acceleration.
rubric.description: Relates acceleration, initial velocity, final velocity and time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either equivalent relation.

rubric.why: Substituting for time and simplifying eliminates time from the displacement equation.
rubric.description: Eliminates time and obtains the intermediate relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution or simplified intermediate result.

rubric.why: This is the third equation of motion.
rubric.description: States the third equation of motion correctly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the final equation.

modelAnswer: For a velocity-time graph with initial velocity u and final velocity v, displacement s is the area under the graph.
s = area of trapezium = 1/2 (u + v)t
Acceleration, a = (v − u)/t, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substituting in the displacement equation: s = 1/2 (u + v)(v − u)/a
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u²
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.

items.followUp: Explain how a hydraulic press multiplies an applied force.

rubric.why: A hydraulic system works because pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally throughout it.
rubric.description: States Pascal's principle or its equivalent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying equal pressure transmission in an enclosed liquid.

rubric.why: The input pressure is the applied force divided by the area of the small piston.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relation.

rubric.why: Equal pressure at both pistons relates their forces and areas.
rubric.description: Relates the forces and areas of the two pistons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: The larger output piston produces a greater force, making the system a force multiplier.
rubric.description: Explains how the larger piston gives a greater output force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the force-multiplier conclusion.

modelAnswer: A hydraulic system consists of two pistons of areas A₁ and A₂ connected by an enclosed liquid.
By Pascal's principle, pressure applied to the liquid is transmitted equally throughout it.
If force F₁ is applied to the small piston, the pressure is P = F₁/A₁.
The same pressure acts on the large piston, so P = F₂/A₂.
Therefore, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, and F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.
Since A₂ is greater than A₁, F₂ is greater than F₁; hence the hydraulic system multiplies force.

rubric.description: Sets up or evaluates the conversion of one year into seconds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct conversion setup or the number of seconds in one year.

rubric.description: Gives the estimated age in seconds.

items.followUp: Give two examples of how friction is useful in everyday life.

rubric.why: Friction between the feet and the ground is needed for walking; without it, the feet slip.
rubric.description: States that walking would be difficult or impossible because feet would slip.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid consequence concerning walking.

rubric.why: Without friction, moving objects would not slow down through friction, and brakes could not stop vehicles.
rubric.description: States a valid consequence for moving objects or vehicles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid consequence concerning continued motion or ineffective braking.

modelAnswer: Without friction, we would not be able to walk because our feet would slip.
Moving objects would continue moving without slowing down, and vehicles could not be stopped by brakes.

items.followUp: Define unstable equilibrium and give one example.

rubric.why: A body in stable equilibrium returns to its original position after a small displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the body returns to its original position after a small displacement.

rubric.why: The question asks for two examples of stable equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both examples.

modelAnswer: A body is in stable equilibrium if, after a small displacement, it tends to return to its original position.
Examples: a ball at the bottom of a bowl, and a book lying on a table.
